summary: EDHOC is a compact, lightweight authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange using ephemeral keys. It provides mutual authentication, forward secrecy, and identity protection. It is meant for constrained scenarios, such as setting up an OSCORE security context. It reuses COSE for cryptography, CBOR for encoding, and CoAP for transport.

eli5.summary: Two tiny gadgets want to agree on a secret handshake without shouting it. EDHOC lets them do so in only a few small messages and prove who they are.

questions: lightweight authenticated key exchange for iot
how many messages does edhoc use
subtitle: A compact authenticated key exchange that lets tiny IoT devices agree on fresh keys in three small messages.

tldr.problem: Constrained IoT devices need an authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange that uses few round trips, tiny messages and little extra code, so that keys for protocols like OSCORE can be set up and refreshed cheaply.
tldr.mechanism: EDHOC exchanges ephemeral public keys in three messages, authenticates each side with a signature key or a static Diffie-Hellman key, and reuses CBOR, COSE and CoAP so existing libraries cover most of the work.
tldr.outcome: It provides mutual authentication, forward secrecy and identity protection, with example exchanges of 101 bytes in total for the smallest static Diffie-Hellman case. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Cipher suites that MUST be supported

today: RFC 9528 is a Proposed Standard, published in March 2024, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Test vectors and annotated traces for it are given in RFC 9529.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Key Exchange
sections.content:
Many Internet of Things deployments are constrained in memory, storage, processing power and energy, and their networks can be lossy, slow or changing. In such settings the number of round trips, the size of each message and the amount of code all matter. Smaller messages fit in fewer radio frames, which cuts fragmentation and latency, and smaller code is easier to ship in firmware updates.

EDHOC (Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE) is designed for exactly this. A main goal is to give OSCORE a lightweight way to authenticate and establish session keys. By reusing CBOR for encoding, COSE for cryptography and CoAP for transport, the extra code size stays very low. EDHOC itself is not tied to a particular transport.

Authentication can use raw public keys or public key certificates. Pre-shared key authentication is not supported, because static Diffie-Hellman public keys referenced by name give equally small messages with simpler key distribution and identity protection. In the RFC's size comparison for raw public keys over CoAP, EDHOC messages can be less than 1/7 of the DTLS 1.3 handshake.
sections.eli5: Little gadgets have tiny backpacks and weak batteries. EDHOC is a handshake that fits in a small backpack, so even a tiny gadget can do it.

sections.title: Three Messages, Two Roles
sections.content:
The two parties are the Initiator (I), who sends message_1, and the Responder (R). Messages are CBOR Sequences, and the odd messages come from I and the even ones from R. There are three mandatory messages, an optional fourth, and an error message that either side can send.

  • message_1 carries METHOD, the cipher suites the Initiator supports, its ephemeral public key G_X, its connection identifier C_I and optional external authorization data.
  • message_2 carries the Responder's ephemeral key G_Y followed by an encrypted part holding C_R, the credential identifier, a signature or MAC, and optional data.
  • message_3 is the Initiator's authenticated and encrypted reply with its own credential identifier and signature or MAC.
  • message_4 is optional and gives the Initiator key confirmation.

The design follows the SIGMA-I family, the same family behind IKEv2 and TLS 1.3, which protects the Initiator's identity against active attackers. EDHOC implements the MAC-then-Sign variant. Both sides keep running transcript hashes (TH_2, TH_3, TH_4) of the data exchanged, which feed into key derivation and into the authentication.

After creating message_3 the Initiator can already derive application keys, so protected application data can be sent in parallel with it. Message_4 is typically not sent.
sections.eli5: One gadget says hello with a secret half-key, the other answers with its half and shows an ID card, and the first shows its ID card back. After that both can build the same secret key.

sections.title: Methods, Credentials and Application Profiles
sections.content:
The METHOD field selects how each side proves itself. Four methods exist: each side uses either a signature key or a static Diffie-Hellman key. Even with static keys, EDHOC always runs an ephemeral-ephemeral key exchange as well. When a static Diffie-Hellman key is used, authentication comes from a MAC computed from an ephemeral-static shared secret, which keeps messages small. EDHOC has no version field; breaking changes are introduced by registering new methods.

Each side has an authentication credential (CRED_I, CRED_R) holding its public key, such as a raw public key wrapped in a CWT Claims Set, a CWT, or an X.509 or C509 certificate. The messages carry an identifier of the credential (ID_CRED_I, ID_CRED_R), a COSE header map. It can hold the credential itself or just a reference such as a kid or an x5t hash, and a lone kid gets a compact encoding. The credential is included in the MAC, so it is integrity protected.

EDHOC proves possession of the private key but leaves other checks, such as whether the credential is trusted, valid and not revoked, to the application. Parameters that both sides must agree on outside the protocol, such as the method, the credential types, the use of message_4 and the transport, are described in an application profile.

Connection identifiers C_I and C_R are byte strings that only help each side find its protocol state. Byte strings that equal a one-byte CBOR integer in the range -24 to 23 are sent as that integer, saving a byte on the wire.
sections.eli5: Each gadget can prove who it is by signing its name or by using a lock-and-key pair it already owns. The application decides whom to trust; EDHOC only checks that the other side really holds the key it showed.

sections.title: Key Derivation and the Exporter
sections.content:
EDHOC uses Extract-and-Expand (HKDF-style). EDHOC_Extract turns shared secrets into pseudorandom keys, and EDHOC_KDF, built on EDHOC_Expand, derives keys, IVs and MACs. The first key, PRK_2e, comes from the ephemeral-ephemeral shared secret with the transcript hash TH_2 as salt, which gives forward secrecy. PRK_3e2m and PRK_4e3m mix in the static Diffie-Hellman secrets when a side authenticates that way, and otherwise equal the previous key.

From these keys come KEYSTREAM_2, the keys and IVs for message_3 and message_4, the MACs, and the final session key PRK_out. Applications do not use PRK_out directly. They call EDHOC_Exporter, which takes an exporter label from a registry, a context and a length. An (exporter label, context) pair MUST NOT be used for two different purposes.

An optional function, EDHOC_KeyUpdate (Appendix H), derives a new PRK_out from the old one for cheap rekeying. It gives forward secrecy but much weaker properties than re-running EDHOC with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman.
sections.eli5: The two gadgets mix their secret halves into a big jar of key paste, then squeeze out separate small keys for each job. Old paste is thrown away so a thief cannot use it later.

sections.title: Message Processing and Protection
sections.content:
Message_2's secret part is encrypted by XORing it with a keystream made by EDHOC_Expand. This only needs to defend against a passive attacker. Message_3 and message_4 use COSE_Encrypt0 with the AEAD algorithm of the selected cipher suite. Inside, a signature (as a COSE_Sign1 signature field) or a MAC over the transcript hash and the credential proves identity.

Each side processes messages in order, and different instances of the same message MUST NOT be processed in one session. The Initiator SHOULD NOT persistently store PRK_out or send protected application data until the application has authenticated the Responder. Where no protected application message flows from the Responder to the Initiator, message_4 MUST be supported and used so that the Initiator gets key confirmation.

Padding can be added through External Authorization Data (EAD) items with label 0. The EAD fields (EAD_1 to EAD_4) carry opaque authorization data defined by other specifications. A negative label means the item is critical, and a receiver that does not understand a critical item MUST send an error and abort. Padding in EAD_1 reduces amplification attacks, and padding in later messages hides the true length.
sections.eli5: Every message is sealed in an envelope that only the other gadget can open, and each seal also covers everything said so far. If anyone changed an earlier note, the seal would not match and the handshake stops.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Errors
sections.content:
A cipher suite is an ordered set of algorithms (EDHOC AEAD, hash, MAC length, key exchange curve, signature, application AEAD and application hash), identified by an integer. The EDHOC MAC length MUST be at least 8 bytes. Suites 0 to 3 use AES-CCM for constrained IoT, 4 and 5 use ChaCha20, 6 uses AES-GCM, and 24 and 25 are for high security uses. Suites 2 and 3 MUST be implemented, and they differ only in MAC length.

The Initiator lists suites in order of preference, with the selected suite last. All suites it prefers over the selected one MUST be included. The Responder accepts only if the selected suite is the first one in the list that it also supports. Otherwise it sends error code 2 with the suites it supports (SUITES_R), and the Initiator can retry with a new message_1. Because the list is bound into the transcript hash, tampering with it is detected and the session aborts, so an attacker cannot force a downgrade.

Errors are fatal. Besides code 2, code 1 carries a diagnostic text string, and code 3 reports an unknown credential reference so that the sender can try a different credential identifier next time. Error messages are not protected and can be forged, so a receiver MAY try to continue.
sections.eli5: The first gadget lists the secret languages it speaks, best first. The other picks the best one both know. If someone tries to trick them into a worse language, the later check fails and they stop.

sections.title: Security Properties and Caveats
sections.content:
EDHOC provides forward secrecy, mutual authentication with aliveness, consistency and peer awareness, in the terms of the SIGMA analysis. Including the credentials in the transcript hash protects against identity misbinding. Identity protection is asymmetric: the Initiator is protected against active attackers and the Responder against passive attackers, so roles should be assigned to protect the more sensitive identity.

The ephemeral keys MUST NOT be reused across messages and both parties SHALL generate fresh random ephemeral key pairs. The hash output size MUST be at least 256 bits and the AEAD tag length at least 64 bits. The RFC says EDHOC gives at least 64-bit security against online brute force and at least 128-bit security against offline brute force. Compromising long-term keys does not compromise completed sessions.

Several things are left to the application and lower layers. EDHOC has no denial-of-service protection of its own; for CoAP the Echo option can force a client to show reachability. EAD_1, EAD_2, ID_CRED_R and error messages are unprotected or only weakly protected and may leak information, and connection identifiers sent in clear can be used for tracking. On post-quantum use, the RFC says only that any KEM can be used in method 0, and that replacing static Diffie-Hellman authentication would likely need a specification that updates EDHOC with new methods.
sections.eli5: The handshake keeps old secrets safe even if a key is stolen later. It cannot stop someone from flooding a gadget with fake hellos, so other layers have to help.

sections.title: Use With OSCORE and CoAP
sections.content:
Appendix A shows the main use case. After message_3, both sides derive the OSCORE Master Secret and Master Salt with EDHOC_Exporter using labels 0 and 1 and an empty context, with a default salt length of 8. The OSCORE Sender and Recipient IDs come from the EDHOC connection identifiers C_R and C_I, swapped between the two roles.

EDHOC over CoAP uses POST requests to /.well-known/edhoc and 2.04 (Changed) responses. In the default forward message flow the CoAP client is the Initiator. Message_1 is prepended with the CBOR value true to mark a new session, and later client messages are prepended with the connection identifier the server chose. A reverse flow, where the server is the Initiator, is also defined. Media types are application/edhoc+cbor-seq and, with a prepended identifier, application/cid-edhoc+cbor-seq. Error responses SHOULD use CoAP code 4.00 or 5.00.
sections.eli5: Once the handshake is done, the gadgets use the new secret to lock their normal CoAP conversation. The handshake itself rides in ordinary CoAP messages to a well-known address.
